display.title: Confessed, Not Said: Precision in the Kinnim Viduy

learning.ahaMoment: Precision matters: 'after he confessed' captures the act of atonement through words, while 'after he said' is merely descriptive.
learning.memoryAnchor: 'Confessed' vs 'said' - the former is the halachic category; the Gemara insists on precision in describing the atoning act.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Gemara insist on saying 'after he confessed' rather than 'after he said,' and what closes out the kinnim discussion?
learning.coreTension: Describing the High Priest's first confession only as 'he said' would describe mere speech, but the formula needs to capture viduy as a halachic act of confession, not just an utterance.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara corrects the language to 'after he confessed' (hitvadeh), establishing that the formula must name the legal category of confession itself, not merely report that words were spoken.

takeaway.text: The formula must say 'after he confessed,' not 'after he said' - confession (viduy) is the legal category that carries atonement, and the Gemara insists the language used to describe it conveys that category precisely.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat 'said' and 'confessed' as interchangeable since both describe speech, missing that only 'confessed' names the halachic act of viduy that carries atonement.

display.title: The Azazel Goat's Organized Journey: Ten Booths to the Tsuk

learning.ahaMoment: The Azazel goat's journey was organized and companioned - not abandoned. The infrastructure of booths reflects the community's active participation in the ceremony.
learning.memoryAnchor: 10 booths = 10 stations = organized ritual journey for the goat, with national support along the way.
learning.learnerQuestion: How was the Azazel goat actually sent to the wilderness, and was it truly abandoned alone?
learning.coreTension: The Torah commands the goat be sent away by the hand of a designated man, but the Mishna's description of ten staffed booths and an accompanying retinue raises the question of how much communal structure surrounded what could be read as a solitary act of abandonment.
learning.coreMove: The Mishna details ten booths from Jerusalem to the Tsuk, each offering the ish iti food and drink and a relay of escorts to the next station, showing the sending was a structured, accompanied journey rather than the goat being left alone from the start.

takeaway.text: The Azazel goat's journey to the Tsuk was an organized, staffed, and escorted procession of ten booths spanning 12 mil, not a solitary abandonment - communal structure surrounded the sending even as the goat itself was finally left alone at the cliff.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may picture the goat as simply turned loose into the wilderness alone, missing the elaborate infrastructure of ten booths, provisions, and escorts that organized its journey.

rashiTranslations.en: What is there to say? But here, it is neither at the time of taking nor the time of performing it
that he establishes it. Do not say 'and afterward he said,' but rather 'and afterward he took it and said.'
This one for the sin-offering and this one for the burnt-offering, for the Sages phrased a stipulation that omits one word, through
forgetfulness, and they thereby confuse between 'and afterward he took' and 'and afterward he said.' And we raise a difficulty:
'he took' - if so, he adds and brings his obligation of an animal
from the money of his sin-offering - what is that? For he
has no money, since he has already bought the bird.
'that he redeems it' - he takes it out to non-sacred status and adds
from his own funds, and buys an animal with the money.
'But there is no redemption for a bird' - for so we learned
in tractate Menachot (100b): but birds,
frankincense, and service vessels have no redemption,
for redemption was stated only regarding an animal. 'Such as
if he took one pigeon' - he took one young dove
from the funds set aside, and this is what the Gemara means:
if he bought a burnt-offering with it, this money that stands
designated for a sin-offering, he adds to it and brings
his obligation, and this burnt-offering that he bought goes to a freewill-offering.
'If he bought a sin-offering' - the remaining money of the fund
becomes fixed for a burnt-offering through this taking, and he does not
add to it and bring his obligation from it; rather,
he brings a freewill burnt-offering from the money, and the sin-offering
that he bought must die, and from his own house he must bring money and take
an animal. 'A leper is different' - for it is written,
(Leviticus 14) 'This shall be the law of the leper,'
and not another. 'The first clause too' - a poor person who brought
the offering of a rich person. 'There, behold, the Torah included' -
one law for all lepers; all of them
fulfill their obligation with a rich person's offering. 'And so it was taught' -
stated affirmatively. 'And let us learn from it' - regarding one who defiles
the Temple. '"But if he is poor"' - this is an exclusion,
teaching that specifically for a leper does a rich person who brought the offering
of a poor person not fulfill his obligation, but the rest of those liable for a sliding-scale
offering - not. 'The mishnah: opposite the place
of its sending away' - opposite the gate through which they took it out
for its sending away. 'And for the one that is slaughtered' - this is explained in the Gemara.
'Does it refer to the tying' - that he ties the thread
to it, opposite its neck. 'Or does it refer to the standing'
- and this is what the Mishnah means: the sin-offering goat
that stands to be slaughtered, he stands it
opposite the place of its slaughtering. 'Well put' -
for then they are not mixed up with one another, since this one has the thread tied
on its head and this one on its neck, and not on others,
since on these the thread is tied, and on the others
it is not tied. 'But if you say' -
'and for the one slaughtered' refers to the standing, and because
the Mishnah speaks of the tying of the sent-away goat alone,
it teaches that they should not be mixed up with one another and not
with others - granted, with the sent-away goat it is not
mixed up with the inner goat, since this one
has the thread tied on it and that one does not have it tied on it; but
with other goats, why would the inner goat not be mixed up
with them? For neither the inner goat nor others
have the thread tied on them. 'Two threads
I have heard' - regarding two scarlet threads
I have heard a distinction between them: one of the red heifer,
about which it is written (Numbers 19), 'and the priest shall take'
'cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool.'
'One requires a measure' - and its measure is explained
below. 'And one does not require a measure' -
for it is fit at any amount. 'That requires division' -
as we learned below (67a): what would
the one who sends away the goat do? He would divide the scarlet thread,
tying half on the rock and tying half between
its horns. 'Requires weight' - so that it be heavy
and fall into the depth of the fire, as it is written
there, 'into the midst of the burning of the heifer.' 'It is a matter of dispute

among tanna'im' - below, in this discussion. 'How does he do it?' - we learned this in tractate Parah (3:11). 'He binds them' - to the cedar wood and hyssop. 'With the remainder of the thread' - since it teaches
'remainder,' it implies there is more.' 'At the tail of the thread' - combed with a comb and made narrow at one end, like a tail. 'That the flame caught them' - and they did not fall into

the burning of the heifer, but were singed in the air. 'And he sanctifies it' - meaning, and places it there; every act of the heifer's preparation is called sanctification. 'With a rising flame' - a fire that has over it a column

of flame standing erect above, like the tall stalk of a plant, in which case one must bring another; and that which R. Chanin said it is fit with a bent flame refers to a fire whose flame is low and bent

and close to its ember, and of it we may read 'into the midst.' 'That they all be in one bundle' - for we require that they be taken together, as it is written, 'and he shall take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet

wool.' 'And one of the leper' - for regarding him too it is written 'scarlet wool and hyssop.' 'And I cannot explain' - and I do not know how to explain which is the largest, which is the smallest, and which is the middling one.
